name: Samarkand
subtitle: Maracanda, Face of the Earth
description: A thousand years of Samarkand between the Siab stream and the Dargom canal: the Sogdian merchant city on the loess plateau of Afrasiyab, the Samanid city of paper and gardens spreading south, and after the Mongol sack of 1220 the new walled city where Timur, Ulugh Beg and the Uzbek khans raised the Registan, Bibi-Khanym and the Gur-e-Amir. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Siab (Siyob)
water.blurb: The 'Black Water': a spring-fed stream that runs round the east and north foot of Afrasiyab to the Zarafshan. Its ravine protected the old city; its current drove the mills, including, by tradition, Samarkand's paper mills.

water.name: Dargom canal
water.blurb: The great canal taken off the Zarafshan east of the city, which watered the gardens of the south side. Arab geographers knew it as the Barsh or Dargham; its course here is approximate.

water.name: Obi-Mashhad ravine
water.blurb: A stream in a deep loess ravine along the west side of Afrasiyab, running north to the Siab; the old city's western moat.

water.name: Ariq of the Ark
water.blurb: One of the ariqs (open irrigation channels) led off the Dargom into the city: each mahalla took its turn of water by day and night.

water.name: Ariq of the Registan
water.blurb: An ariq running north toward the Registan. One explanation of the name Registan, 'sandy place', is the silt such channels left on the square.

water.name: Eastern ariq
water.blurb: An irrigation channel feeding the gardens and pools of the east side of the city.

water.name: Ariqs of the rabad
water.blurb: Channels from the Dargom running north through the suburbs; Istakhri says almost every house and garden of Samarkand had running water.

hills.name: Afrasiyab
hills.blurb: A plateau of loess about 220 hectares, cut off by ravines and the Siab: the site of Samarkand from the 7th century BCE to the Mongol sack of 1220, named in later legend after the Turanian king of the Shahnameh. Abandoned afterwards to graves and fields.

hills.name: Kohak (Chupan-ata spur)
hills.blurb: The 'little mountain', a spur of the Chupan-ata hills across the Siab, where Ulugh Beg built his observatory and Timurid princes kept the Bagh-i Maydan garden.

hills.name: Hill of Hazrat Khizr
hills.blurb: A loess knoll by the old south gate of Afrasiyab, crowned by a mosque since early Islamic times.

roads.name: Street of the Kesh gate
roads.blurb: From the citadel south to the Kesh gate (Bab al-Kish), the way to the rabad and to Kesh (Shahrisabz). The modern road through Afrasiyab runs close to it.

roads.name: Street of the China gate
roads.blurb: Across the inner city from the Nawbahar gate in the west to the China gate (Bab al-Sin) in the east.

roads.name: Road to Kesh
roads.blurb: South through the rabad and across the Dargom toward Kesh and the passes to Bactria: the main street of the suburbs.

roads.name: Road to Bukhara
roads.blurb: West down the Zarafshan valley to Bukhara: the caravan route to Merv and Iran.

roads.name: Road to Ustrushana and China
roads.blurb: East up the valley toward Panjikant, Ustrushana and the passes to Ferghana and China.

roads.name: Street of the rabad
roads.blurb: A street of the outer city running west among the gardens.

roads.name: Timur's bazaar street
roads.blurb: From the Registan to the Iron Gate past Bibi-Khanym. In 1404 Timur had it cut through the houses and lined with shops under a vaulted roof in some twenty days, working by night and day (Clavijo).

roads.name: Road to Shah-i-Zinda
roads.blurb: From the Iron Gate along the foot of Afrasiyab to the street of tombs.

roads.name: Road to Kohak
roads.blurb: Out past Shah-i-Zinda and across the Siab to the observatory hill and the Bagh-i Maydan.

roads.name: Street of the Karizgah gate
roads.blurb: South from the Registan to the Karizgah gate and on to Kesh, Timur's birthplace.

roads.name: Road to Shahrisabz
roads.blurb: Across the Dargom toward Kesh, which Timur renamed Shahr-i Sabz, the Green City.

roads.name: Street of the Chorsu
roads.blurb: West from the Registan through the Chorsu crossing to the gate of the Ark.

roads.name: Street of the Bukhara gate
roads.blurb: From the Chorsu north-west to the Bukhara gate.

roads.name: Road to Bukhara
roads.blurb: The caravan road west to Bukhara, 250 km down the Zarafshan.

roads.name: Street of the Shaykhzada gate
roads.blurb: North-west from the Registan to the Shaykhzada gate; gate names after Sharaf al-Din Yazdi and Clavijo, positions approximate.

roads.name: Street of the Firuza gate
roads.blurb: East from the Registan to the Turquoise gate (Firuza) and the roads to the garden palaces.

roads.name: Road to the gardens
roads.blurb: Out to the garden palaces and the meadow of Kan-i Gil on the Siab, where Timur pitched his tents.

roads.name: Street of the Sozangaran gate
roads.blurb: South-east to the gate of the needle-makers (Sozangaran).

roads.name: Road south-east
roads.blurb: Toward the villages up the Dargom and the road to Panjikant.

walls.name: Walls of Afrasiyab
walls.blurb: Several lines of pakhsa and mud-brick ramparts round the plateau, rebuilt from the 6th century BCE to the 12th century CE; four gates in Arab times: Nawbahar (west), Bukhara (north), China (east) and Kesh (south).

walls.name: Ramparts of Afrasiyab (ruined)
walls.blurb: Breached by the Mongols in 1220 and never rebuilt: eroded loess ramparts round an empty plateau of mounds, potsherds and graves.

walls.name: Wall of the rabad
walls.blurb: The outer wall round the suburbs, with many gates, described by Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal; its line is drawn here schematically. Beyond it a still longer wall enclosed the gardens and villages.

walls.name: Walls of Timur's city
walls.blurb: Mud-brick walls with a moat, built round the new city in the 1370s and joined to the Ark on the west. Six gates: Ahanin (Iron), Firuza, Sozangaran, Karizgah, Bukhara and Shaykhzada; their positions here follow the usual reconstruction.

bridges.name: Bridge over the Dargom
bridges.blurb: Where the road to Kesh crossed the great canal south of the city.

bridges.name: Bridge over the Dargom
bridges.blurb: The crossing of the Dargom on the road to Shahrisabz.

bridges.name: Bridge over the Siab
bridges.blurb: A crossing of the Siab on the way to the meadows and garden palaces east of the city.

bridges.name: Bridge to Kohak
bridges.blurb: The crossing of the Siab below the observatory hill.

bridges.name: Bridge at the China gate
bridges.blurb: Where the road east crossed the Siab below the China gate.

blocks.name: Mahallas south of the Firuza street

gardens.name: Garden lands east of the Siab

districts.name: Afrasiyab (the shahristan)
districts.description: The walled inner city on its loess plateau: citadel, palace, temple and later the Friday mosque, and merchants' quarters along the four streets from the gates.

districts.name: Afrasiyab (ruins)
districts.description: The old city, deserted after the Mongol sack of 1220: mounds of melted mud brick, a few graves and the shrines on its southern slope.

districts.name: The rabad
districts.description: The outer city south of Afrasiyab: markets, caravanserais, mosques, gardens and workshops, and the residence of the Samanid governors.

districts.name: Timur's city
districts.description: The walled city of the 1370s, roughly today's old town: mahallas of courtyard houses round the Registan, with the Ark on the west and Bibi-Khanym by the north gate.

districts.name: Shah-i-Zinda
districts.description: The necropolis of the 'Living King', Qutham (Kusam) ibn Abbas, on the southern slope of Afrasiyab, where Timur's family and amirs built their tombs.

districts.name: Kohak
districts.description: The hill of the observatory and the Bagh-i Maydan garden north-east of the city.

periods.label: Sogdian Samarkand
periods.summary: Maracanda of Alexander's historians, now the chief city of Sogdiana, ruled by its ikhshid kings under loose Turkic and Chinese overlordship. The walled city covers the loess plateau of Afrasiyab: a citadel on the north point, a temple, merchants' houses with painted halls. Sogdian traders run the caravan routes from Iran to China. Mud brick and pakhsa (rammed loess), timber columns, painted plaster.
periods.feel: Sogdian, Turkic and Chinese in the bazaar, fire altars and painted gods, camels loading silk and musk at the gates, lutes and wine at a merchant's feast.

houses.title: Sogdian merchants' houses
houses.text: Two-storey houses of pakhsa and mud brick packed along narrow lanes; the richest had a square reception hall with four wooden columns, benches along the walls, and paintings of gods, heroes and banquets covering every wall.

outskirts.title: Vineyards and estates
outskirts.text: Below the plateau, irrigated vineyards, orchards and the fortified farmhouses (kushk) of landowners, fed by channels from the Zarafshan; villages of craftsmen along the Siab.

periods.label: Samanid Samarkand
periods.summary: Taken by the Arabs in 712, Samarkand becomes a great Islamic city under the Samanids (819–999) and the Karakhanids. Afrasiyab is the walled inner city with four gates and the Friday mosque by the citadel; a vast walled suburb (rabad) of markets and gardens spreads south. The city makes paper, sells it across the caliphate, and drinks from a lead-lined canal. Sacked by the Mongols in 1220.
periods.feel: Water running in lead channels and open ariqs, the thud of paper-mill hammers on the streams, Persian and Arabic in the mosques, slave and silk caravans at the gates.

houses.title: Houses of the rabad
houses.text: Single and two-storey courtyard houses of mud brick with flat roofs of beams, reeds and clay; plastered halls carved with stucco; a pool or a channel in the yard. Istakhri says nearly every house had a garden and running water.

outskirts.title: Gardens of Sughd
outskirts.text: Geographers called the valley of Sughd one of the four paradises of the earth: orchards, vineyards, melon fields and summer houses as far as the eye could see from the citadel.

periods.label: Timur's capital
periods.summary: Old Afrasiyab, sacked in 1220, lies empty; the city has moved south. Timur (r. 1370–1405) made it his capital, walled it in the 1370s and filled it with the spoils and craftsmen of his conquests. In 1404 Clavijo, envoy of Castile, finds the Bibi-Khanym mosque just built, the Gur-e-Amir ready for Timur's grandson, and the tents and garden palaces of the court outside the walls.
periods.feel: Scaffolds and elephants at the great mosque, glazed tiles stacked in the lanes, horse meat and melons for the feast, the drums of the court in the meadow of Kan-i Gil.

houses.title: Mahallas of Timur's city
houses.text: Mud-brick courtyard houses with flat earth roofs, an ayvan porch on carved wooden columns facing the court, a pool and a vine; each mahalla with its own small mosque and well. Clavijo thought the city a little larger than Seville.

outskirts.title: Garden suburbs
outskirts.text: Outside the walls Clavijo found more houses than within, and the great gardens of Timur and his family, each walled, with a palace, pools and avenues of trees.

periods.label: Ulugh Beg's Samarkand
periods.summary: Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg governs Samarkand from 1409 and makes it a city of science: a madrasa on the Registan (1417–1420), a khanaqah and caravanserai round the square, and the great observatory on the Kohak hill (c. 1428–1429), where his astronomers compile a new star catalogue. He is murdered in 1449; the Timurid princes quarrel over the city.
periods.feel: Students reciting in the madrasa cells, the glint of the meridian arc on Kohak, scholars arguing mathematics in Persian, the din of the Registan market.

houses.title: Mahallas round the Registan
houses.text: Dense one- and two-storey courtyard houses of mud brick and timber, flat-roofed, with ayvans and carved doors; workshops of potters, weavers and coppersmiths grouped by trade in their own mahallas and bazaars.

outskirts.title: Gardens and shrines
outskirts.text: Garden palaces kept by the princes, the meadows of the Kohak hill, and the tombs and khanaqahs that grew up along the roads out of the gates.

periods.label: Samarkand of the Uzbek khans
periods.summary: The Uzbek Shaybanids take Samarkand in 1500; later Bukhara becomes the capital and Samarkand a provincial seat under its Janid (Ashtarkhanid) khans. The governor Yalangtush Bahadur completes the Registan with the Sher-Dor (1619–1636) and Tilya-Kori (1646–1660) madrasas. The observatory is a ruin, Bibi-Khanym decaying.
periods.feel: Tigers and suns blazing on the new portal, gold leaf in the Tilya-Kori mosque, pigeons in the cracked dome of Bibi-Khanym, caravans thinner than before.

houses.title: Uzbek mahallas
houses.text: Courtyard houses of mud brick on timber frames, with a men's outer court and a women's inner court, ayvans on carved columns, flat clay roofs where people slept in summer; a guzar square with a mosque, a pool and a teahouse-like gathering place.

outskirts.title: Fields and orchards
outskirts.text: Much of the old walled area and the Timurid gardens returned to orchards, melon fields and cemeteries; villages along the canals.

landmarks.name: Registan

samanid-950.note: Gardens and lanes of the rabad, the outer city south of Afrasiyab. The square does not yet exist.

timur-1404.name: Registan (the market square)
timur-1404.note: The 'sandy place': an open market square where the new city's main streets meet, ringed with stalls and a domed covered market. Timur's grand building went elsewhere; the square waits for his grandson.

ulughbeg-1440.note: Ulugh Beg's madrasa (1417–1420) stands on the west side, facing his khanaqah on the east; a caravanserai closes the north. The square is the scholarly and commercial heart of the city.

shaybanid-1650.note: Yalangtush Bahadur replaces the decayed khanaqah with the Sher-Dor (1619–1636), mirroring Ulugh Beg's facade, and the caravanserai with the Tilya-Kori madrasa and Friday mosque (1646–1660): three portals round one square.

landmarks.summary: The public square of Timurid and Uzbek Samarkand, framed by three madrasas with huge tiled portals: Ulugh Beg's (1417–1420), the Sher-Dor (1619–1636) and the Tilya-Kori (1646–1660).
details: Ulugh Beg's madrasa was a college of some fifty cells round a court, with domed lecture halls at the corners and four minarets. It taught theology but also astronomy and mathematics; tradition says Ulugh Beg lectured there himself. Its 35-metre portal is covered in glazed mosaic of stars and geometric bands.

The miniature shows the facades with their pishtaqs framed in bands of turquoise, cobalt and white tile, the corner minarets and the ribbed domes. In 1404 the square is a reconstruction of a market place; the 1650 Sher-Dor's famous tigers and suns are only suggested by the tile panels in its spandrels.
landmarks.function: Market square; madrasas and Friday mosque

landmarks.name: Bibi-Khanym Mosque

samanid-950.note: Houses and gardens of the rabad below the Kesh gate of Afrasiyab.

timur-1404.name: Masjid-i Jami of Timur
timur-1404.note: Just finished, or nearly so: begun in 1399 with the plunder of Delhi, built by masons from Iran, Azerbaijan and India, its stones hauled by elephants. Timur, back in 1404, had the portal rebuilt higher.

ulughbeg-1440.note: The city's Friday mosque, already showing cracks: the vaults had been built too fast and too big, and bricks fell from the dome while the faithful prayed below, as later writers tell.

shaybanid-1650.name: Bibi-Khanym (decaying)
shaybanid-1650.note: Tilya-Kori has taken over as the Friday mosque. The great dome is cracked and partly fallen, the minarets broken; how far the ruin had gone by 1650 is uncertain.

landmarks.summary: Timur's congregational mosque, one of the largest of the Islamic world, built in five years after his Indian campaign with a 35-metre portal, a 40-metre dome and four corner minarets round a vast court.
details: Begun in May 1399 and completed about 1404, the mosque measures about 167 by 109 metres. A huge portal opens on a court with a domed hall at each side and the main sanctuary at the end under its turquoise ribbed dome; minarets stand at the four corners. It later took the name of Timur's chief wife, Saray Mulk Khanum.

The miniature shows the portal with its octagonal minarets, the court with arcades and side domes, and the main dome on its tall drum, all faced in brick with glazed blue patterns. The ruined variant follows its decay, whose stages before the 1897 earthquake are poorly dated.

landmarks.name: Gur-e-Amir

timur-1404.note: Built for Timur's favourite grandson and heir, Muhammad Sultan, who died in 1403, beside the madrasa and khanaqah he had founded. Clavijo saw it; within months Timur himself would lie here.

ulughbeg-1440.note: Ulugh Beg has added the gallery and the outer portal and laid over Timur's grave a great block of dark green nephrite, brought from Mughulistan in 1425. He will be buried here in 1449.

shaybanid-1650.note: The Timurid family tomb, its madrasa decayed but the dome and tombs kept as a shrine; the madrasa side and khanaqah are falling into ruin.

landmarks.summary: The 'Tomb of the Ruler': the mausoleum of Timur, his sons and grandsons, with its famous fluted turquoise dome on a tall drum, built 1403–1404.
details: An octagonal tomb chamber under a double dome: the outer dome, about 15 metres across with 64 ribs, sits on a drum written round with giant Kufic letters in white and blue. Inside, gilded and painted walls and the cenotaphs of Timur, Muhammad Sultan, Shah Rukh, Miran Shah and Ulugh Beg; the bodies lie in a crypt below.

The miniature shows the tomb at the south of a court entered from the north through a tiled portal, flanked by the remains of Muhammad Sultan's madrasa and khanaqah, with a minaret at the corners. The court's original layout is simplified.

landmarks.name: Shah-i-Zinda

samanid-950.note: Outside the Kesh gate, the grave of Qutham ibn Abbas, cousin of the Prophet, said to have come with the first Arab raids; Samarkandis already venerated it, though the shrine was modest.

timur-1404.note: Timur's sisters, nieces, wives and amirs have built a lane of tombs up to Qutham's shrine since the 1360s: Shadi Mulk Aka (1372), Shirin Beka Aka (1385), Tuman Aka (1405 in progress).

ulughbeg-1440.note: Ulugh Beg adds the lower gateway (1434–1435) and the double-domed mausoleum traditionally said to be that of his teacher Qazi-zada Rumi at the foot of the street.

shaybanid-1650.note: Still the city's holiest place: pilgrims climb the steps to Qutham's shrine, and Uzbek nobles add graves among the Timurid tombs.

landmarks.summary: The 'Living King': a street of glazed mausolea climbing the southern slope of Afrasiyab to the shrine of Qutham ibn Abbas, where Timur's family were buried.
details: The legend says Qutham, beheaded by unbelievers, took up his head and went down into a well where he lives still. His shrine drew a necropolis: in the 14th and 15th centuries Timur's relatives and amirs lined the path with tombs whose facades are among the finest tilework in Islam, carved and glazed terracotta in turquoise, cobalt and white.
The miniature shows the stepped lane climbing from the lower gateway past tight rows of domed tombs with tiled portals to Qutham's complex at the top. The number and order of tombs is simplified.

landmarks.name: Ulugh Beg Observatory

timur-1404.note: An empty hilltop of Kohak above the Siab, among the meadows where Timurid princes kept gardens.

ulughbeg-1440.note: Built about 1428–1429: a three-storey round building whose heart is a vast meridian arc, used to measure the sun's height and the year. Here al-Kashi, Qazi-zada Rumi and Ali Qushji worked.

shaybanid-1650.name: Ruins of the observatory
shaybanid-1650.note: Abandoned after Ulugh Beg's murder in 1449 and pulled down for its bricks; by 1650 only a mound on the hill. The arc's trench was rediscovered by Vasily Vyatkin in 1908.

landmarks.summary: Ulugh Beg's observatory on the Kohak hill: a round building about 46 metres across holding a meridian arc of some 40 metres radius, where the Zij-i Sultani star tables were made.
details: The building rose in three storeys about 30 metres high round the great instrument, the Fakhri sextant: a marble-faced arc set in a trench cut into the rock along the meridian, graduated to measure the sun's and stars' altitudes. The observers produced a catalogue of 1,018 stars and a length of the year within a minute of the true one.

The miniature shows the cylinder with its arcades of niches and the arc rising through the roof. The upper storeys and the outer decoration are known only from excavation and brief descriptions, so they are a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Citadel of Afrasiyab

sogdian-650.name: Citadel of the ikhshid
sogdian-650.note: The fortress and palace of the kings of Samarkand on the north point of the plateau, with a keep, halls of pakhsa and mud brick, and towers over the Siab ravine.

samanid-950.name: Quhandiz of Samarkand
samanid-950.note: The citadel holds the prison and the governor's offices; the Samanid governors live in the rabad. The Karakhanids later build a painted palace here in the 12th century.

timur-1404.name: Ruins of the old citadel
timur-1404.note: Stormed by the Mongols in March 1220 and left in ruins. Timur's city lies two kilometres south; the old citadel is a mound of melted brick.

ulughbeg-1440.name: Ruins of the old citadel
ulughbeg-1440.note: A ruin mound above the Siab, quarried for earth and brick.

shaybanid-1650.name: Ruins of the old citadel
shaybanid-1650.note: A ruin mound above the Siab; the name Afrasiyab, from the legendary Turanian king, is now attached to the whole plateau.

landmarks.summary: The fortress on the north point of Afrasiyab, seat of the Sogdian kings and later of governors, stormed by the Arabs in 712 and destroyed by the Mongols in 1220.
details: The citadel stood on the highest ground of the plateau, above the Siab ravine, with its own walls and a keep. Excavations found the Sogdian palace levels and, above them, a Karakhanid palace of the late 12th century with wall paintings of warriors and hunters.
The miniature shows the walled citadel with towers, the keep and palace halls; its layout is a reconstruction from excavated fragments. After 1220 it appears as a ruined mound.

landmarks.name: Hall of the Ambassadors

sogdian-650.note: A noble's reception hall painted about 660 under King Varkhuman: envoys from Chaghanian, Chach, China and Korea on the west wall, a Chinese princess in a boat, a royal procession with an elephant.

samanid-950.name: Buried hall
samanid-950.note: Burned or abandoned after the Arab conquest and built over; the paintings lay buried until road builders found them in 1965.

landmarks.summary: The square painted hall of a Sogdian residence on Afrasiyab, whose murals of about 660 show foreign embassies coming to King Varkhuman: the 'Ambassadors' Painting'.
details: The room, about 11 metres square, had benches along the walls and paintings on all four sides. A Sogdian inscription on the west wall names Varkhuman and an envoy of the king of Chaghanian; two envoys in feathered caps are usually identified as Koreans of Goguryeo. Varkhuman is known from Chinese annals as a king appointed by the Tang about 658.

The miniature shows a Sogdian house with a columned portico and the square hall under a flat roof with a lantern. The outside of the building is a reconstruction; only the lower walls and the paintings survive, now in the Afrasiyab Museum.
landmarks.function: Reception hall of a Sogdian residence

landmarks.name: Friday Mosque of Afrasiyab

sogdian-650.name: Temple of Samarkand
sogdian-650.note: A walled temple court with a columned hall and a fire sanctuary, where the Sogdians kept images of their gods. Its exact plan is unknown; this is the usual interpretation of the excavated levels.

samanid-950.note: The Friday mosque of the inner city beside the citadel, rebuilt and enlarged under the Samanids: a court and a hypostyle hall of wooden columns with a brick minaret.

timur-1404.name: Ruins of the old mosque
timur-1404.note: Burned in the Mongol assault of 1220 and abandoned with the rest of Afrasiyab.

landmarks.summary: The congregational mosque of the inner city, built after 712 on the site of the Sogdian temple next to the citadel and rebuilt several times before 1220.
details: Tabari tells that the conqueror Qutayba ibn Muslim had the idols of Samarkand burned in 712 and a mosque built. Excavations beside the citadel found a large mosque with several building phases from the 8th to the 12th century, of mud brick with wooden columns.

The miniature shows a court with a deep hall of wooden columns under a flat roof and a minaret; the Sogdian variant shows a walled temple court with a portico and a raised sanctuary. Both are interpretations of fragmentary remains.

landmarks.name: Ark and Kok Saray

samanid-950.note: Gardens and estates on the western edge of the rabad.

timur-1404.note: Timur's citadel on the west of the city with the four-storey Kok Saray, the 'Blue Palace': treasury, armoury, workshops and prison. Timur himself preferred to live in his gardens and tents.

ulughbeg-1440.note: Ulugh Beg's seat of government. In the Kok Saray, tradition says, the Timurid rulers were raised on a slab of grey stone, the Kok Tash.

shaybanid-1650.note: The Uzbek governors' citadel. The Kok Saray is said to have been decaying; the Ark survives as a fortress into the 19th century.

landmarks.summary: Timur's citadel on the western side of the walled city, with the Kok Saray ('Blue Palace'), his treasury and the government of the empire.
details: The Ark was walled separately from the city, with its own gates. Within it Timur built the Kok Saray, a palace of several storeys named for its blue tiles, and the Bustan Saray. Contemporaries describe treasuries, workshops of armourers and a prison where princes were kept.

The miniature shows the walled Ark with towers, a gate toward the city and the tall tiled block of the Kok Saray; the Russian fortress later built on the site destroyed the remains, so the layout is a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Rukhabad Mausoleum

timur-1404.note: Built about 1380 over the grave of the holy man Burhan al-Din Sagharji: a plain brick dome, the 'abode of the spirit', among the mahallas near the Ark.

ulughbeg-1440.note: A place of pilgrimage within sight of the Gur-e-Amir's blue dome.

shaybanid-1650.note: Still a shrine, its dome unrepaired brick among the houses.

landmarks.summary: An early Timurid mausoleum of plain brick, built about 1380 for the sheikh Burhan al-Din Sagharji, with a portal and a smooth dome on an octagonal drum.
details: A square chamber with a projecting portal on the south, octagonal drum and dome, all in unglazed fired brick with almost no tile: a sober contrast to the Timurid tombs that followed. Legend says a casket with hairs of the Prophet was buried with the sheikh.
The miniature shows the cube, drum and dome in buff brick; proportions follow the standing building.

landmarks.name: Ak Saray Mausoleum

ulughbeg-1440.note: Houses and gardens south-east of the Gur-e-Amir; the Ak Saray will be built here in the 1470s.

shaybanid-1650.note: A late Timurid tomb, probably of the 1470s, perhaps for princes of the dynasty; inside, walls painted in gold and blue, outside a low dome over a cross-shaped hall.

landmarks.summary: A late Timurid mausoleum near the Gur-e-Amir, built about 1470, famous for its painted and gilded interior; its patron and occupants are uncertain.
details: The building is a cross-shaped hall under a dome with a crypt below; the exterior was never fully faced. The interior painting in kundal technique, raised gilded relief on blue, is among the finest of its age.
The miniature shows the brick cube with shallow portals and a low dome. The original outer dome is lost; its height is a guess.

landmarks.name: Hazrat Khizr Mosque

sogdian-650.note: A knoll outside the Kesh gate; tradition puts a pre-Islamic shrine here.

samanid-950.note: Said to be one of the first mosques of Samarkand, built in the 8th century by the Kesh gate on the site of an older shrine, and dedicated to al-Khidr, the green prophet of travellers.

timur-1404.note: Burned with Afrasiyab in 1220; a mosque on the knoll serves travellers at the Iron Gate. Its form in this period is unknown.

ulughbeg-1440.note: A small mosque on its hill above the road to Shah-i-Zinda.

shaybanid-1650.note: A small neighbourhood mosque. The present building, with its painted ayvan, dates from 1854.

landmarks.summary: A small mosque on a knoll by the old south gate of Afrasiyab, by tradition one of the first in Samarkand and dedicated to al-Khidr, patron of travellers.
details: The tradition of an 8th-century mosque here, on a pre-Islamic sacred site, is old but unproven; the mosque was rebuilt after the Mongol sack and again in 1854, when it took its present form with a domed hall, an ayvan on carved columns and a small minaret.
The miniature shows a domed prayer hall with a columned ayvan and a small minaret, a type common in Samarkand; it stands for a building whose medieval form is not known.

landmarks.name: Siab Bazaar

samanid-950.note: Lanes of the rabad just below the Kesh gate, where the Juy-i Arziz canal crossed into the inner city.

timur-1404.note: Stalls, sheds and a domed hall outside the Iron Gate, where the produce of the villages came in: melons, grapes, bread, horses and hides. Its medieval form is not recorded; this is a reconstruction.

ulughbeg-1440.note: The market at the north gate, between Bibi-Khanym and the road to Shah-i-Zinda.

shaybanid-1650.note: The market of the north side, busy with peasants from the Siab villages.

landmarks.summary: The market at the north gate of the walled city, between Bibi-Khanym and Afrasiyab, still Samarkand's main bazaar today.
details: Samarkand's bazaar at the Iron Gate grew with the Timurid city; Clavijo marvelled at the plenty of meat, bread, fruit and melons sold in the squares. The present market dates from the 20th century but keeps the site.
The miniature shows a walled yard of stalls under awnings round a small domed hall and a pool; the layout is a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Chorsu

timur-1404.note: The crossing just east of the Registan where the roads to Tashkent, Bukhara and Shahrisabz met, probably already a market; its form here is a reconstruction.

ulughbeg-1440.note: Hatters, cloth sellers and money changers under the dome.

shaybanid-1650.note: A domed market at the crossing; the hexagonal Chorsu that stands now was built in the late 18th century.

landmarks.summary: The 'four ways': a domed market building over a crossing of bazaar streets just east of the Registan.
details: Central Asian cities covered the crossings of their main bazaar streets with domed halls (chorsu or tim), lit through the drum and lined with shops. Samarkand's surviving Chorsu was built in the late 18th century; it was paid for by the Bukharan emir Shah Murad. A market stood at this crossing earlier, but an older domed building here is not documented.
The miniature shows an octagonal domed hall with four arched entrances and shops round it, in the manner of the Timurid and Shaybanid trading domes of Bukhara.

landmarks.name: Bagh-i Dilkusha

timur-1404.note: The 'Heart-Gladdening Garden', laid out in 1397: a walled square garden of avenues, pools and a palace with a tiled gateway. Timur received the Castilian envoys here; its position is approximate.

ulughbeg-1440.note: Kept by the Timurid princes as a pleasure garden; Ulugh Beg preferred the gardens near Kohak.

shaybanid-1650.name: Lost garden
shaybanid-1650.note: The garden palaces of Timur had gone back to fields and orchards; only their names survived.

landmarks.summary: One of Timur's garden palaces outside Samarkand: a walled square garden with a pavilion, pools and avenues, laid out in 1397 for his marriage to a Mongol princess.
details: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi describes Timur's gardens round the city, each a walled square crossed by avenues and channels with a palace at the centre; the Dilkusha's walls were said to bear paintings of his Indian campaign. Clavijo was received in gardens like this, with tents of silk, pools and orchards.
The miniature shows a four-part garden with a tiled gatehouse, a central pavilion on a raised platform, pools and trees. The exact site, east of the city toward Kan-i Gil, is uncertain.

spots.name: House of a Sogdian silk merchant
spots.summary: A two-storey house of pakhsa off the street of the Nawbahar gate, whose owner trades silk, musk and silver between Samarkand, the Turks and Chang'an.
details: Sogdian merchants worked in family firms with agents in every caravan town to China; letters in Sogdian found in Dunhuang and Turfan record their deals. At home they received guests in a painted hall with benches, under images of gods, the hero Rustam and banquets, as excavated houses at Panjikant show.

vignettes.text: Servants sweep the yard and feed the household fire; in the hall the painted Nana rides her lion above the benches.
An agent back from Turfan unrolls a bill of sale for a slave girl and bolts of silk; the master counts silver drachms with a Chinese clerk.
Lamps, harp and wine: a feast for partners from Chach, with a Sogdian whirling dancer, the kind Tang poets wrote about.

spots.name: Caravan halt at the China gate
spots.summary: A yard below the eastern gate where caravans to and from Ferghana and China unload, water camels in the Siab and pay the gate tolls.
details: Samarkand stood where the routes from Iran, India and the steppe met the road east; its merchants spread Sogdian as the trade language of the Silk Road. Arab geographers counted the caravanserais of the rabad among its wonders.

vignettes.text: Bactrian camels groan as they kneel; drivers in felt hats check the ropes on bales of raw silk from the east.
A tax-collector weighs a sack of musk pods while a Turkic escort waits on horseback.
Fires in the yard, mutton on skewers, stories of the Tian Shan passes in three languages.

samanid-950.name: Caravanserai at the China gate
samanid-950.note: Now a brick caravanserai with rooms round a yard; the goods are paper, cloth, slaves from the steppe and Chinese silk.

spots.name: Naus (ossuary vaults)
spots.summary: Small domed vaults outside the walls where Sogdians placed clay ossuaries holding the bones of their dead, cleaned by birds and dogs as Zoroastrian custom required.
details: Sogdian Zoroastrians did not bury or burn bodies but exposed them, then kept the bones in ossuaries, boxes of fired clay often stamped with figures of priests and fire altars. Many have been found round Samarkand; the cemetery placed here is illustrative.

vignettes.text: A family carries a painted ossuary up the path; inside, the bones of a grandmother, gathered after the year's exposure.
Heat shimmers over the low domes; kites circle above the ravine.
A lamp left burning in a niche, a little fire for the soul's journey over the Chinvat bridge.

spots.name: Christian church of the rabad
spots.summary: A church of the Church of the East, whose metropolitan sat at Samarkand by the 8th century; its place in the city is not known.
details: Syriac sources name a metropolitan of Samarkand, and Christian Sogdians left texts, crosses and coins. Ibn Hawqal mentions a Christian monastery near the city. The building drawn here is placed for illustration only.

vignettes.text: Syriac psalms in a small brick church; the deacon is a Sogdian, the priest trained in Merv.
A merchant leaves a silver cross as a gift before setting out for the east.
The gate is shut; inside, a lamp before the altar and a book of Gospels in Sogdian.

sogdian-650.note: Christians are a small community among Zoroastrians, Buddhists and Manichaeans; whether they had a church in the city is uncertain.

spots.name: Paper mill on the Siab
spots.summary: Water-driven hammers pounding rags and flax into pulp beside the Siab: the paper of Samarkand, prized from Baghdad to Cairo.
details: Samarkand was the first city of the Islamic world known for paper; al-Tha'alibi in the 11th century counted it among the city's specialities, said to have replaced papyrus and parchment. The mills on the streams east of the city still worked into the 19th century; one has been revived at Konigil.

vignettes.text: The wheel turns and the trip hammers thud; a boy feeds soaked linen rags under them.
Sheets lifted on a sieve frame, pressed, then burnished with a stone until they shine for the scribe's reed.
Bales of paper tied for Baghdad stand by the door; the stream runs on in the dark.

timur-1404.note: Samarkand paper is still the best in Timur's empire, used by the chancery and the copyists of the court.

shaybanid-1650.note: Paper making continues on the streams round the city, though Bukhara now has the court.

spots.name: Ras al-Taq market
spots.summary: The great market of the rabad just outside the Kesh gate, where Istakhri says most of the city's trade was done.
details: The Arab geographers describe the inner city as having few markets and the rabad as full of them, with the Ras al-Taq as the busiest. Samarkand exported paper, silver cloth, copper pots, stirrups and, notoriously, Turkish slaves bought on the steppe.

vignettes.text: Water-sellers fill skins from the lead canal's overflow; bakers' ovens already smoke.
A coppersmith hammers a basin; a slave-dealer parades boys from the steppe destined for the Samanid guard.
Stalls shuttered; the watch walks the lanes with torches.

spots.name: Potters of Afrasiyab
spots.summary: Kilns where potters made the white slipware of Samarkand, written round with Arabic proverbs in black or red.
details: Samanid epigraphic pottery, found in quantity at Afrasiyab, carries sayings such as 'Knowledge is bitter to taste at first, but sweeter than honey in the end' in elegant Kufic, on a creamy white slip.

vignettes.text: A boy treads clay in a pit; the master throws a deep bowl on the wheel.
A calligrapher-potter brushes a proverb round the rim, the letters stretched tall like a palisade.
The kiln glows; tomorrow the bowls go to the market and on to Nishapur.

spots.name: Timur's tents at Kan-i Gil
spots.summary: The meadow east of the city along the Siab where Timur held his great feasts and weddings in 1404 among a city of silk tents.
details: Clavijo describes the tents of the court pitched in the meadow: one great pavilion of silk with four masts, walls of coloured cloth, and feasts where whole horses and sheep were served and the guests drank till they fell. The Kan-i Gil meadow lay further east than drawn here.

vignettes.text: Grooms water horses in the Siab; craftsmen of each trade build their stalls for the festival, each guild trying to outdo the others.
Roasted horse and mutton in great leather dishes; the Castilian envoys are seated below the envoy of China, and the old emir laughs.
Musicians, wine, fires; executions, Clavijo adds, were also part of the festival's justice.

spots.name: Timur's new bazaar street
spots.summary: The vaulted shopping street Timur had cut through the city in 1404, from the Registan toward Bibi-Khanym, in about twenty days.
details: Clavijo tells how Timur, finding the city's markets too cramped, ordered a street to be driven straight through the houses, their owners crying out but getting no redress, with shops on both sides and a roof with skylights; the work went on by day and night.

vignettes.text: Demolition dust over the lane: gangs knock down a house while the owner argues with an amir's officer.
Under the new vault, light falls from openings onto cloth of Damascus, Chinese satin and Russian furs.
Torches and drums: the work continues all night, as Timur ordered.

ulughbeg-1440.note: The covered street is now the city's main bazaar, its shops let by the waqf of the great mosque.

shaybanid-1650.note: Still the bazaar street to the north gate, though many of its vaults have been rebuilt.

spots.name: Quarter of the deported craftsmen
spots.summary: Workshops of silk weavers, armourers, glassmakers and potters whom Timur brought from Damascus, Iran, India and Anatolia to build and furnish his capital.
details: Clavijo lists the craftsmen Timur had carried off: from Damascus weavers of silk, bow-makers, armourers, glass and porcelain makers; from Turkey crossbowmen and masons; from elsewhere gunsmiths and rope-makers. Sharaf al-Din names the masons and tile-cutters of Tabriz and Shiraz who worked on his buildings.

vignettes.text: A Syrian weaver sets his loom for a velvet patterned with gold; his children already speak Turkic.
Tile-cutters from Shiraz chip turquoise and cobalt pieces into stars for the mosque, fitting them face down into a plaster bed.
An Indian stonemason sits with his countrymen and remembers Delhi, sacked five years ago.

ulughbeg-1440.note: The deported families are now Samarkandis; their sons cut the mosaics of Ulugh Beg's madrasa.

spots.name: Melon market at the Karizgah gate
spots.summary: Heaps of melons brought in from the fields south of the city, so many in autumn, Clavijo says, that they were cut in strips and dried to keep through the winter.
details: Clavijo marvelled at the melons of Samarkand, large and sweet, and at the drying of their flesh like figs. Babur later praised the melons of the region above all others.

vignettes.text: Ox-carts creak in from the Dargom fields, piled with green and golden melons.
A seller slaps a melon to show its ripeness and slices it for you; the juice runs down your wrist.
Strips of melon hang drying on cords across a roof, pale gold in the lamplight.

spots.name: Non baker's tandir
spots.summary: A mahalla bakery where round flat loaves (non) are slapped onto the inside wall of a clay tandir oven, stamped with patterns in the middle.
details: Samarkand's thick, glossy non is still famous in Central Asia. Tandir ovens have been found at Afrasiyab and are used across the region; the details of the bread in Timurid times are not recorded, so this spot is illustrative.

vignettes.text: The baker's arm disappears into the glowing tandir and the dough sticks to the wall; the first loaves come out shining with milk.
A child carries a stack of loaves home on her head, wrapped in a cloth.
The oven cools; the baker's apprentice stamps tomorrow's loaves with a nail-studded stamp.

spots.name: Ulugh Beg's bath
spots.summary: A domed public bath near the Registan, traditionally said to have been built by Ulugh Beg (the 'Hammam-i Mirzo').
details: Babur describes a bath built by Ulugh Beg in Samarkand called the Mirza's bath, paved with stones of many kinds. Its position is not certain; it is placed here for illustration.

vignettes.text: Steam rising from the domes; the stoker feeds the furnace with dried dung and brushwood.
Under the star-pierced dome, a masseur cracks a merchant's joints on the warm marble.
Women's hours: talk, henna and the news of the court.

spots.name: A student's cell in Ulugh Beg's madrasa
spots.summary: One of the small domed rooms round the madrasa court where two students lived, studied and slept, with a niche for books and a hearth.
details: A letter of the mathematician al-Kashi to his father describes Samarkand's scholarly life: Ulugh Beg teaching in the madrasa, crowded lectures, and the sultan questioning scholars on mathematics. The madrasa taught astronomy and mathematics beside law and theology.

vignettes.text: Prayer in the mosque hall, then cold bread and water; a student copies tables of sines by the door for the light.
In the corner lecture hall a teacher reads Euclid; the sultan himself has come to listen and asks a sharp question.
Two roommates argue over the motion of the moon by the light of a clay lamp.

shaybanid-1650.note: The madrasa still teaches, but law and theology now; the observatory's science is a memory.

spots.name: Caravanserai outside the Bukhara gate
spots.summary: A walled brick inn on the Bukhara road with rooms round a court, stabling for camels and storerooms for cloth, paper and dried fruit.
details: Caravanserais lined the roads into every Central Asian city; Samarkand's trade with Bukhara, Herat, India and Russia passed through them. This one stands for many whose exact sites are not known.

vignettes.text: The gate creaks open; a caravan for Bukhara forms up in the road, bells clanking.
An Indian merchant spreads indigo and muslin on a rug for a Samarkand buyer.
The gate is barred; on the roof, drivers sleep under the stars beside their loads.

shaybanid-1650.note: Trade continues, though the ocean routes have drawn off some of the long-distance goods; caravans now go mostly to Bukhara, India and Russia.

events.title: Varkhuman receives the embassies
events.text: King Varkhuman, confirmed by the Tang emperor as governor of 'Kangju', receives envoys from Chaghanian and Chach, and, the painter shows, from China and Korea. The scene is painted on the west wall of a nobleman's hall, with a Sogdian inscription naming the king.

events.title: Qutayba takes Samarkand
events.text: After a siege, the Arab general Qutayba ibn Muslim forces the ikhshid Ghurak to surrender. Tabari tells that Qutayba had the idols piled up and set alight himself, and gold nails were found in the ashes; a mosque is built and an Arab garrison installed.

events.title: Talas and the legend of paper
events.text: After the Abbasid victory over a Tang army on the Talas river, Chinese prisoners are said to have taught paper making in Samarkand. The story comes from later writers and paper may have reached Sogdiana earlier, but Samarkand paper became famous across the Islamic world.

events.title: The Mongols take Samarkand
events.text: Chinggis Khan's army besieges the city of the Khwarazm-shah. The townspeople open the gates after a few days; the citadel holds out and is stormed. The people are driven out, craftsmen deported east, many killed; Afrasiyab is never rebuilt.

events.title: Timur makes Samarkand his capital
events.text: Having defeated his rival Amir Husayn at Balkh, Timur is proclaimed ruler and chooses Samarkand as his capital. He walls the city, builds the Ark and the Kok Saray, and for thirty-five years pours the wealth of his conquests into it.

events.title: The great mosque begun
events.text: Back from sacking Delhi, Timur lays the foundation of a Friday mosque to surpass any other. Sharaf al-Din counts some two hundred stonemasons and five hundred labourers, and ninety-five elephants hauling stone.

events.title: Clavijo before Timur
events.text: The envoys of Henry III of Castile are led through a garden to the old emir, seated on cushions before a fountain with red apples bobbing in it. Timur, nearly blind, has them brought close to see them, asks after 'his son the King of Spain', then feasts them.

events.title: Timur's body comes home
events.text: Timur dies at Otrar on 18 February 1405, setting out to conquer China. His body, embalmed with musk and rosewater, is brought to Samarkand and laid in the tomb he had built for his grandson Muhammad Sultan.

events.title: Ulugh Beg's madrasa opens
events.text: On the Registan the young governor's madrasa is finished: four minarets, domed lecture halls and a portal of glazed stars. He appoints Qazi-zada Rumi as head teacher and gathers astronomers and mathematicians from all over Iran.

events.title: The Sultan's star tables
events.text: Ulugh Beg's observers complete the Zij-i Sultani, with a catalogue of over a thousand stars measured afresh, the first such since Ptolemy. Al-Kashi has died before its completion; Ali Qushji finishes the work.

events.title: Ulugh Beg murdered
events.text: Defeated by his own son Abd al-Latif, Ulugh Beg sets out on pilgrimage and is beheaded on the way. He is buried in the Gur-e-Amir at Timur's feet; the observatory is abandoned. Abd al-Latif is killed within six months.

events.title: Babur takes Samarkand
events.text: The fourteen-year-old Timurid prince Babur takes his ancestor's capital after a seven-month siege and holds it for a hundred days. He later describes its buildings with longing in his memoirs, written in India.

events.title: Shaybani Khan takes the city
events.text: The Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani seizes Samarkand. Babur recaptures it by surprise that autumn but loses it in 1501; Timurid rule in Transoxiana is over.

events.title: The Sher-Dor rises
events.text: Yalangtush Bahadur, governor of Samarkand, begins a madrasa opposite Ulugh Beg's, finished in 1636. Its portal shows tigers chasing deer beneath suns with human faces, a rare departure from the usual avoidance of living figures on religious buildings.

stories.title: With Clavijo in Timur's Samarkand
stories.summary: Follow the Castilian envoy Ruy González de Clavijo through the autumn of 1404, from his audience with the old conqueror to the feasts, the new mosque and the bazaar street.

steps.title: An audience in a garden
steps.text: Led by the arms through a gate of blue and gold tiles, the envoys kneel before Timur, seated before a fountain. He calls them closer: his eyes are failing. Then a feast of roast horse and mutton.

steps.title: The meadow of tents
steps.text: In the meadow east of the city the court celebrates weddings among hundreds of silk tents. Every craft builds a pavilion; wine flows; Clavijo notes the gallows set up as well.

steps.title: The great mosque
steps.text: Clavijo tells how Timur judged the portal of his new mosque too low, had it pulled down and rebuilt, and was carried there each day in a litter, throwing meat to the workers to make them hurry.

steps.title: A street in twenty days
steps.text: To give the city a worthy market, Timur orders a street driven through the houses from end to end, with shops and a vaulted roof. Owners who complain get nothing.

steps.title: The captive craftsmen
steps.text: Clavijo counts the craftsmen gathered from conquered cities: silk weavers and armourers of Damascus, glassmakers, masons from Turkey and Iran. Samarkand, he writes, is crowded with them.

steps.title: The prince's tomb
steps.text: Beside the madrasa of the dead heir Muhammad Sultan a tall tomb with a ribbed dome stands ready. Clavijo leaves Samarkand in November; by March 1405 Timur lies here.

stories.title: Ulugh Beg's city of stars
stories.summary: A day in the scholar-prince's Samarkand: from the madrasa on the Registan to the meridian arc on Kohak, as described in the letters of al-Kashi.

steps.title: The madrasa on the square
steps.text: Ulugh Beg's madrasa faces his khanaqah across the Registan. Al-Kashi wrote that the prince came to lectures and discussed problems of geometry with the students himself.

steps.title: A cell of two students
steps.text: Behind the portal, small domed rooms round the court; students copy star tables and argue over the Almagest by lamplight.

steps.title: The Mirza's bath
steps.text: Babur later remembered the bath Ulugh Beg built, paved with many kinds of stone. Scholars and merchants meet in the steam.

steps.title: Timur's jade
steps.text: At the family tomb, the dark green nephrite slab Ulugh Beg brought from the steppe in 1425 covers his grandfather's grave.

steps.title: Up the street of tombs
steps.text: Through Ulugh Beg's new gateway, past the double-domed tomb said to be Qazi-zada Rumi's, to the shrine of the Living King.

steps.title: The arc on the hill
steps.text: On Kohak the great sextant is cut into the rock. At noon the sun's image falls through an opening onto the marble arc, and the astronomers read off its height with unusual precision.
